title: Classical Planning (STRIPS & PDDL)
html:
Planning finds a sequence of actions that achieves a goal, using a factored representation: states are sets of facts and actions are schemas with preconditions and effects. That structure allows domain-independent heuristics that make planners scale to huge problems.

The STRIPS representation

PartMeaningBlocks world
StateConjunction of ground facts (fluents); everything else is false (closed world)On(C, A) ∧ OnTable(A) ∧ OnTable(B) ∧ Clear(C) ∧ Clear(B)
GoalConjunction of facts that must hold (a partial state)On(A, B) ∧ On(B, C)
Action schemaName, preconditions, add list, delete listMove(b, x, y)

An action is applicable when its preconditions hold; its result is (state − delete list) ∪ add list. Facts not mentioned stay unchanged — this is how STRIPS sidesteps the frame problem. PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) is the standard modern syntax:

Forward (progression) planning

Treat planning as search: states are fact sets, successors come from applicable ground actions. Here is the Sussman anomaly — start with C on A; goal A on B on C:

Key point

The Sussman anomaly defeats planners that achieve goals one at a time: stacking A on B first (after clearing C) must be undone to get B onto C, and achieving B on C first buries A. The goals interact, so a planner must interleave them.

Search strategies and heuristics

ApproachIdea
Forward (progression) searchFrom the initial state apply applicable actions. Many irrelevant actions — needs a good heuristic.
Backward (regression) searchFrom the goal, consider only relevant actions (that add a goal fact without deleting another); regress the goal through them. Smaller branching factor.
Ignore-delete-lists heuristicSolve the relaxed problem where actions never remove facts (the basis of FF and HSP planners). Admissible variants give A*-optimal plans.
Ignore-preconditions heuristicCount how many actions are needed if any action could always be applied — roughly the number of unsatisfied goals.
Planning graphs / GraphPlanLayered graph of reachable facts and actions with mutex links; the level where all goals first appear is a heuristic estimate.
SAT planningEncode “is there a plan of length T?” as a Boolean formula and hand it to a SAT solver.

Partial-order planning

A partial-order planner (POP) searches in the space of plans, not states, and commits to an ordering only when necessary (least commitment). A plan has actions, ordering constraints A ≺ B, and causal links A →p→ B (A achieves precondition p of B). A threat is an action that could delete p between A and B — resolved by ordering it before A (demotion) or after B (promotion).

Least commitment

Putting on shoes: RightSock ≺ RightShoe and LeftSock ≺ LeftShoe, but the left and right sides are unordered — the plan allows any of the 6 interleavings.

Beyond classical planningHandles
Hierarchical task networks (HTN)High-level actions refined into sub-plans — how most real planners (and games' NPCs) work
Scheduling with resourcesDurations, deadlines, limited machines/crew — critical-path method
Contingent / conformant planningPartial observability: plans with sensing actions and branches
Replanning & execution monitoringDetect when the world deviates from the plan and repair it
MDPs (next group)Stochastic action outcomes — a policy instead of a fixed sequence
What is STRIPS?

A planning representation where states are sets of ground facts and each action has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. Anything not mentioned is unchanged, which avoids writing frame axioms. PDDL is its modern, more expressive successor.

Forward vs backward state-space planning?

Forward search starts from the initial state and applies applicable actions — simple but branches on many irrelevant actions. Backward (regression) search starts from the goal and only considers relevant actions, giving a smaller branching factor, but works on sets of states and makes heuristics harder.

Why can planning use domain-independent heuristics while plain search cannot?

The factored representation exposes the structure of actions, so a planner can automatically build relaxed problems — ignoring delete lists or preconditions — and solve them to get heuristic estimates without any domain-specific coding.
